title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: AG Nessel seeks 71% cut to DTE hike; data centers fuel the fight

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're looking at Attorney General Dana Nessel's call for a big reduction in DTE's rate hike request, with data center power demand right in the middle of it.
Graham, walk me through what Nessel actually asked for today.
She told regulators the full $474 million increase would hit households too hard and wants it cut by 71 percent.
That's a huge swing. Why is she drawing such a hard line?
Nessel argues the full hike would burden families already dealing with rising costs, and she singled out data center demand as one key driver behind DTE's request.
How exactly are data centers pushing this? We've been tracking the buildout for months.
These facilities need enormous amounts of reliable power, often around the clock, and southeast Michigan is seeing multiple large proposals at once.
So if the hike gets approved even at a smaller level, what does that mean for monthly bills?
A smaller hike would still mean higher rates for everyone, from Detroit to Ann Arbor and beyond, because the grid has to expand to meet the new load.
What's the history here? Has DTE been signaling this for a while?
Yes, the utility has pointed to retiring coal units and surging demand from data centers and other large users as reasons it needs new capacity.
And yesterday we heard about DTE planning two new gas plants for exactly this reason.
Right, those plants would add fossil fuel generation and likely push customer bills higher if regulators approve them.
What about water and land impacts? Data centers aren't just about electricity.
Cooling systems pull significant water, and large sites often convert farmland or open land, which is why towns like Saline and others are rewriting rules.
How many communities are feeling this pressure right now?
At least a handful in Metro Detroit and West Michigan have updated zoning or extended moratoriums this week alone.
Let's shift to those quick hits. First, the new state bills on data centers.
Lawmakers introduced measures yesterday to add oversight on power use, noise, and local tax deals for big projects.
Who benefits most if those pass?
Residents in communities facing rapid development could get tighter local control, but developers say it could slow investment.
Next, the recall effort that failed.
A clerk rejected petitions yesterday against officials who approved rezoning for a 500-acre project, so that development stays on track.
Tough break for opponents. What happens next there?
Residents opposed to the power use and tax breaks now face a steeper climb to force another vote.
Saline Township is still moving forward too.
Yes, the project advances even as officials tighten zoning under resident pressure, bringing construction jobs but also heavy utility demands.
And folks 30 miles away will feel it through rates?
Exactly, because the power and tax shifts ripple across the region.
Two more suburbs rewrote rules yesterday.
Metro Detroit towns updated zoning codes after noise, water, and power concerns, which could slow or block projects developers had eyed.
Wixom got sued over blocking one.
A developer is taking the city to court, claiming the zoning decision unfairly killed its plans, which could mean taxpayer costs if it drags on.
Solon Township extended its freeze.
Leaders recommended keeping the moratorium through early next year while they update rules on noise, traffic, and utility costs.
And the West Michigan town did the same.
That community pushed its ban out to at least early 2027 so residents can study the impacts before anything moves forward.
Finally, the decibel study in Gaines Township.
Officials will measure sound levels at the proposed site to see if cooling fans and generators would disturb nearby homes.
That data could actually halt or reshape the project.
Homeowners within a few miles now have a concrete way to judge the noise impact.
On deck this weekend, are there any public meetings listeners can attend?
No major hearings listed for tonight or tomorrow, but several townships are still updating zoning codes behind the scenes.
Where should people check for the latest agendas?
The Michigan Data Center Tracker has the live map and meeting notices as they come in.
Anything else on the calendar for early next week?
We'll keep an eye on any follow-up regulatory filings from DTE and the new state bills as they move through committees.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Nessel Pushes Major Cut to DTE Rate Hike as Data Centers Drive Demand
